<reason>B wins by distinguishing housing disinflation from actual affordability and making the instrument’s costs central: tighter credit can damage renters’ earnings and housing construction without resolving scarcity. A offers plausible concerns about leverage and exclusion, but never establishes its decisive assumption that income losses are temporary while housing relief lasts. B also cleanly distinguishes warranted broad-inflation tightening from an independent housing priority, exposing the burden behind A’s willingness to tighten even when overall inflation is at target.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s pressure question forced A to concede that prices could rebound after rates fall. B then showed that A’s fallback—a buyer avoiding peak mortgage debt—does not establish lasting relief for distressed renters facing higher borrowing costs and unemployment risk. This directly undermined A’s central temporary-pain-versus-permanent-benefit comparison.</best_rebuttal>
